Iron fortification of staple food is a strategy utilized worldwide to address the concern of dietary iron deficiency. However, traditional salt-based fortification methods have limitations with gastrointestinal stability and bioavailability. Iron chelating peptides from easily available and scalable proteins such as whey protein have been proposed as promising candidates to circumvent the above mentioned limitations by enhancing iron absorption and bioavailability.
Furthermore, reduction in the antioxidant property of peptides following iron complexing indicates iron chelation. Our results suggest that whey protein derived peptide-iron complexes can be used as a potential alternative for chemical iron fortificants for food products and also as iron supplements.
These bioactive peptides are specific amino acid sequences in the protein which are released by hydrolysis with enzyme from their parent proteins (Mann, Athira, Sharma, Kumar, & Sarkar, 2019) or produced by digestive enzymes in vitro or in vivo (during gastrointestinal digestion) and exert different physiological effects such as angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibition (Tavares et al., 2011), antidiabetic (Nongonierma & FitzGerald, 2013) and antioxidant activity (Peng, Xiong, & Kong, 2009) and mineral binding property (Guo et al., 2014). Of considerable interest, in recent years, several studies have reported the mineral binding properties of whey proteins (Caetano-Silva et al., 2015, Gandhi et al., 2019, Zhao et al., 2015, Zhou et al., 2012) suggesting their potential to be used in mineral-chelating peptides preparation.
The peptides released during hydrolysis of whey proteins with alcalase showed potent iron-chelating properties. Zeta potential measurement showed that these peptides are highly negatively charged and this property is directly related to the extent of complex formation with iron. Unique absorption peaks of CO-Fe bonds in FTIR spectra of complexes confirmed the involvement of acidic amino acids and their side-chain carboxylic groups for chelation.
